sentences.text: Nél took the shoe seriously in the way that only somebody eleven can take a thing seriously.
She measured it.
It was fourteen centimetres, which she looked up, which made it roughly a size five, which made it a child of about eighteen months to two years.
It was leather, and it had been blue, and it was now the colour of a blue thing that has spent a long time somewhere.
It had a strap and a small button and the button was still on.
Somebody, at some point, had put a stitch into the strap by hand with a thread that did not match, which Nél found harder to look at than anything else about it.
She thought about that stitch a great deal.
It was not a repair the shoe needed.
She looked at it closely, several times, and the strap was not torn and had never been torn.
Somebody had put a stitch into a strap that was perfectly fine, in the wrong colour, by hand.
Which meant somebody had done it after.

On the wall, or in a kitchen, or in the harbourmaster's drawer — somebody at some point in seventy years had picked this thing up and sat down with a needle and put one stitch into it for no practical reason whatsoever.
Nél asked four adults and none of them knew, and two of them looked at her differently for asking.
She was, at first, entirely certain of what it meant.
She was eleven and she had read books.
She took this theory to her father, who put down what he was doing, which he did not usually do.
"No," he said.
"No.
Nobody drowned.
Not a child, not ever, not in this harbour.
I want you to hear that properly." "How do you know?" "Because it's a harbour town and that is precisely the kind of thing a harbour town knows to the exact date." He picked his work back up.
"There's a list in the church with every soul this water has taken since 1804 and it is not a long list and there is not a child on it.
You can go and read it.
I did, when I was about your age, for the same reason." Nél went and read it.
It took her forty minutes and she was quiet for two days afterwards, but not the kind of quiet she had been expecting.
The list was cut into two slate panels on the north wall inside the door, and it ran from 1804 to 1998, and there were sixty-one names on it.
She had expected to be frightened by it.

What she actually felt, working down it with her finger, was something more complicated and a great deal more useful: that all sixty-one had been men, and all sixty-one had been at work, and that the water in that harbour had never once taken anybody who was not being paid to be on it.
She recognised nineteen of the surnames.
Four of them were in her class.
She came out and sat on the church steps for a while.
Then she went down to the harbour and looked at the shoe again, and it had completely changed, and she has never been able to explain to anybody how a thing changes when nothing about it has moved.
